CHAPTER V.

CIRCULAR FUNCTIONS, OR TRIGONOMETRICAL RATIOS.

Function. When one magnitude or ratio is so connected with another that the former changes with the latter, but is determinable for any given value of the latter, the former is said to be a function of the latter.

Hence certain ratios, which depend on the value of the angle, or its circular measure, are called circular functions.

Let \(ACA'C'\) be any circle, \(O\) its centre, \(A'OA\), \(COC'\) two diameters at right angles dividing the circle into four quadrants.

Let \(OA\), \(OC\) be the \(+\) directions for lines measured from \(O\) along these lines respectively. Let \(OA\) be taken as the initial line for angles, and \(ABC\) the \(+\) direction for angles measured from \(OA\). Let \(R\) be the radius of the circle, and \(\theta\left(\dfrac{AB}{R}\right)\) be the circular measure of \(AOB\).

. Sin \(\theta\). The sine of the angle \(AOB\) is the ratio to the radius of the perpendicular from the end of the arc subtending the angle on the initial line \(OA\), \(\therefore \sin\theta = \dfrac{BD}{R}\).

If the position of \(B\) be above the line \(AOA'\), \(\sin\theta\) is \(+\); if below, \(\sin\theta\) is \(-\).

. Cos \(\theta\). The cosine of an angle is the sine of its complement, or \[\cos\theta = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right).\]

Conversely \[\sin\theta = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right).\]

The angle \(AOB\) being \(\theta\), and \(COA = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \[COB = \frac{\pi}{2} - \theta;\] therefore \[\cos\theta = \sin COB = \frac{BE}{R} = \frac{OD}{R}.\]

Hence, if \(OD\) is measured towards \(A\), or if \(B\) lie to that side of \(COC'\), \(\cos\theta\) is \(+\); if \(OD\) is measured towards \(A'\), or if \(B\) lies on the same side of \(COC'\) as \(A'\), \(\cos\theta\) is \(-\).

Variation of the Sine and Cosine. We may examine how the values of these two functions change with the variation of the angle.

When \(AB\) is small, \(BD\) is small and \(+\); \(OD =\) the radius nearly and \(+\). As \(\theta\) increases from \(0\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(BD\) and \(OD\) remain both \(+\), but \(BD\) increases from \(0\) to \(R\), and \(OD\) decreases from \(R\) to \(0\); therefore \[\begin{gather*} \sin\theta \text{ increases from } +0 \text{ to } +1; \\ \cos\theta \text{ decreases from } +1 \text{ to } 0. \end{gather*}\]

As \(\theta\) increases from \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(\pi\), \(BD\) remains \(+\), but diminishes from \(+R\) to \(0\); also \(OD\) becomes \(-\), and \(-OD\) increases from \(0\) to \(+ R\); therefore \[\begin{gather*} +\sin\theta \text{ decreases from } +1 \text{ to } 0; \\ -\cos\theta \text{ increases from } 0 \text{ to } +1. \end{gather*}\]

As \(\theta\) increases from \(\pi\) to \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), \(BD\) becomes \(-\), and \(-BD\) increases from \(0\) to \(+R\); also \(OD\) is \(-\), and \(-OD\) decreases to \(0\); so that \[\begin{gather*} -\sin\theta \text{ increases from } 0 \text{ to } +1; \\ -\cos\theta \text{ decreases from } +1 \text{ to } 0. \end{gather*}\]

As \(\theta\) increases from \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) to \(2\pi\), \(-BD\) decreases to \(0\); and \(+OD\) increases to \(+R\), so that \[\begin{gather*} -\sin\theta \text{ diminishes from } +1 \text{ to } 0; \\ +\cos\theta \text{ increases from } 0 \text{ to } +1. \end{gather*}\]

After this the values from \(2\pi\) to \(4\pi\) are the same as from \(0\) to \(2\pi\): and if \(m\) be any whole number \[\begin{align*} \sin\theta &= \sin(2m\pi + \theta); \\ \cos\theta &= \cos(2m\pi + \theta). \end{align*}\]

If equal angles, \(+\theta\) and \(-\theta\), be measured in opposite directions from \(OA\), and the other ends of the arcs subtending them be joined by the straight line \(BB'''\), \(AOA\) will bisect \(BB'''\) at right angles in the point \(D\).

Therefore the sines of these two angles will be equal but of opposite sign, and their cosines will be equal in sign as well as magnitude; or \[\begin{align*} \sin(-\theta) &= -\sin\theta;\\ \cos(-\theta) &= +\cos\theta. \end{align*}\]

If \(A' B'\), \(A' B''\) be arcs, each \(= AB = R\theta\), but measured from \(A'\); the circular measure of the angles subtended by \(AB'\), \(AB''\) are respectively \(\pi - \theta\), \(\pi + \theta\); and the perpendicular \(B'D' = + BD\), \(B''D = - BD\), and \(OD' = - OD\). Consequently \[\begin{align*} \sin (\pi - \theta) &= \sin\theta, & \cos(\pi - \theta) &= -\cos\theta;\\ \sin (\pi + \theta) &= -\sin\theta, & \cos(\pi + \theta) &= -\cos\theta. \end{align*}\]

And, since both sine and cosine remain unchanged when the angle is increased by a multiple of \(2\pi\) (say by \(2m\pi\)), we have \[\begin{align*} &\sin(2m\pi + \theta)= +\sin\theta; \\ &\sin(-\theta) = \sin(2m\pi - \theta) = -\sin\theta; \\ &\sin(\pi - \theta) = \sin\bigl((2m + 1) · \pi - \theta\bigr) = +\sin\theta; \\ &\sin(\pi + \theta) = \sin\bigl((2m + 1) · \pi + \theta\bigr) = -\sin\theta. \\ \\ \text{ And} &\cos(2m\pi + \theta) = +\cos\theta; \\ &\cos(-\theta) = \cos(2m\pi - \theta) = + \cos\theta;\\ &\cos(\pi - \theta) = \cos\bigl((2m + 1) · \pi - \theta\bigr) = -\cos\theta; \\ &\cos(\pi + \theta) = \cos\bigl((2m + 1) · \pi + \theta\bigr) = -\cos\theta. \end{align*}\]

By these the sine and cosine of an angle of any magnitude can be obtained from the sine or cosine of an acute angle.

It should be observed that, while the number \(\theta\) continuously increases, the numbers \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) pass through a series of values between \(+1\) and \(-1\), and return to the same values again for every increase of \(2\pi\) in the value of \(\theta\). They are therefore said to be periodic functions of \(\theta\), of which the period is \(2\pi\).

Since the perpendicular from the centre of a circle on any chord bisects it at right angles, the ratio of the chord to the radius is twice the sine of half the angle subtended by the chord.

Hence, if we can calculate the ratio to the radius of the side of an inscribed polygon, the sine of half the angle subtended by the side is at once known.

For instance, the side of a square inscribed in a circle \(= R\sqrt{2}\), and it subtends an angle of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) or \(90°\). Therefore

\[\sin \frac{\pi}{4} = \sin 45° = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2} = \cos 45° = \cos \frac{\pi}{4}.\]

The side of the hexagon inscribed is \(= R\), and it subtends \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) or \(60°\). Therefore \[\sin \frac{\pi}{6} = \sin 30° = \frac{1}{2} = \cos 60° = \cos \frac{\pi}{3}.\]

The side of the inscribed equilateral triangle \(= R\sqrt{3}\), and it subtends \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) or \(120°\). Hence \[\sin \frac{\pi}{3} = \sin 60° = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{3} = \cos 30° = \cos \frac{\pi}{6}.\]

The side of the regular decagon inscribed is (Euc. IV. 10, and II. 11) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}R\), and it subtends an angle \(\dfrac{\pi}{5}\) or \(36°\). Hence \[\sin \frac{\pi}{10} = \sin 18° = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{4} = \cos \frac{4\pi}{10} = \cos 72°.\]

. Tan \(\theta\). The tangent of an angle is the ratio to the radius of the part of the line, touching at the initial end the

arc subtending the angle, intercepted between the point of contact and the radius produced through the other end of that arc. In the diagram \[\tan\theta = \frac{AF}{R} \text{ and } AF = R\tan\theta.\]

If \(AF\) be measured towards \(T\), it is to be considered \(+\), and \(-\), if in the contrary direction towards \(T'\).

. Cot \(\theta\). The cotangent of an angle is the tangent of the complement of the angle. Whence \[\cot\theta = \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) \text{ and } \tan\theta = \cot \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right).\]

The cotangent may hence be geometrically defined as follows. Let \(OC\) be drawn perpendicular to \(OA\). Then \(COB\) is the complement of \(AOB\), or \(COB = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\). If \(AOB\) be greater than \(AOC\), or \(\theta > \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(COB\) will be measured from \(CO\) in the other direction, and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\) will be \(-\) to correspond.

Draw \(H'CH\) touching the arc subtending the complement of \(\theta\) at the point \(C\), which is always an extremity of that arc, and through the other extremity of the arc produce the radius to meet it; the tangent of the complement, or cotangent, is the ratio to the radius of the part of \(HCH'\) intercepted. In the diagram \[\cot\theta = \frac{CG}{R} \text{ and } CG = R\cot\theta.\]

If \(CG\) is measured in the direction from \(C\) to \(H'\) the cotangent is \(-\).

Variation of the Tangent and Cotangent. In the first quadrant, when the angle is indefinitely small, the tangent is indefinitely small, and the cotangent indefinitely great; since \(AF\) diminishes, and \(CG\) increases without limit, as \(AOB\) decreases. Hence it is usually said that \(\tan 0 = 0\), and \(\cot 0 = \infty\).

As the angle increases to \(90°\), \(AF\) increases and \(CG\) decreases, both drawn in the \(+\) direction; so that \(\tan\theta\) increases and \(\cot\theta\) decreases, as \(\theta\) increases from \(0\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), and when \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(\tan\theta = \infty\), \(\cot\theta = 0\).

In the second quadrant, where \(\theta\) increases from \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(\pi\), \(AF'\) is measured in the \(-\) direction \(AT'\), and \(CG'\) in the \(-\) direction \(CH'\) for an angle \(AOB'\): so that \(\tan\theta\) and \(\cot\theta\) are both \(-\).

Also, \(AF'\) decreases from an indefinitely great distance in the direction \(AT'\), when \(\theta\) barely exceeds \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), to \(0\) when \(\theta = \pi\); while \(CG'\) increases from \(0\) to an indefinitely great distance in the direction \(CH'\). Hence, as \(\theta\) increases from \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(\pi\), \(-\tan\theta\) decreases from \(\infty\) to \(0\) and \(-\cot\theta\) increases from \(0\) to \(\infty\).

In the third quadrant, or when \(\theta\) increases from \(\pi\) to \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), the lines \(AF\) and \(CG\) are again measured in the positive direction, and the tangent and cotangent are therefore both \(+\), and vary in magnitude as in the first quadrant.

In the fourth quadrant, where \(\theta\) is greater than \(\dfrac{3 \pi}{2}\), and less than \(2 \pi\), the lines are again drawn in the \(-\) direction, and the tangent and cotangent vary just as in the second quadrant.

If two equal angles, as \(AOB\) and \(AOB'''\), or \(AOB'\) and \(AOB''\), be measured in opposite directions from \(OA\), it is obvious that their tangents and cotangents are equal in magnitude, but opposite in sign; or \[\tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta; \text{ and } \cot(-\theta) = -\cot\theta.\]

Also if \(A'OB'\) and \(AOB\) are equal angles, so that \(AOB'\) and \(AOB\) are supplementary, their tangents and cotangents are equal, but of opposite signs; that is \[\tan(\pi - \theta) = -\tan\theta; \quad \cot(\pi - \theta) = -\cot\theta.\]

If \(m\) be any whole number, it is clear that the angle \(2m\pi + \theta\) begins and terminates at the same point as the angle \(\theta\). Therefore, \[\begin{gather*} \begin{aligned} &\tan(2m\pi + \theta) = \tan\theta; & &\cot(2m\pi + \theta) = \cot\theta, \\ &\tan(2m\pi - \theta) = -\tan\theta; & &\cot(2m\pi - \theta) = -\cot\theta. \end{aligned} \\ \begin{aligned} &\tan\bigl((2m + 1) · \pi - \theta\bigr) = -\tan\theta; & &\cot\bigl((2m + 1) · \pi - \theta\bigr) = -\cot\theta, \\ &\tan\bigl((2m + 1) · \pi + \theta\bigr) = \tan\theta; & &\cot\bigl((2m + 1) · \pi + \theta\bigr) = \cot\theta. \end{aligned} \end{gather*}\]

Whence the tangent and cotangent of any angle can be found from those of an acute angle.

. Sec \(\theta\). The secant of an angle is the ratio to the radius of the initial radius produced to meet the tangent at the other end of the arc subtending the angle.

. Cosec \(\theta\). The cosecant is the secant of the complement.

In the diagram, \(AOB\) being the angle, and \(COB\) the complement, \(KS\) the tangent at \(B\); \[\begin{gather*} \sec\theta = \frac{OS}{R};\quad \cosec\theta = \frac{OK}{R}; \\ OS = R\sec\theta;\quad OK = R\cosec\theta. \end{gather*}\]

When \(\theta\) is between \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), \(\sec\theta\) is \(-\), and \(-\sec\theta\) decreases from \(\infty\) (when \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)) till \(-\sec\pi = 1\), and then increases again till \(-\sec\dfrac{3\pi}{2} = \infty\); after which, while \(\theta\) increases from \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) to \(2\pi\), \(+\sec\theta\) decreases from \(\infty\) to \(1\).

Similarly \(\cosec\theta\) is \(+\) in the first and second quadrants diminishing from \(\cosec 0 = \infty\) till \(\cosec\dfrac{\pi}{2} = +1\) and then increasing till \(\cosec\pi = +\infty\).

In the third and fourth quadrants \(\cosec\theta\) is \(-\), and \(-\cosec\theta\) decreases from \(\infty\) at the beginning of the third quadrant till \(-\cosec\dfrac{3\pi}{2} = 1\), and then increases till \(-\cosec 2\pi = \infty\).

. Versin \(\theta\). The versed sine of an angle is the ratio

to the radius of the part of the initial radius (produced if necessary) which is intercepted between its extremity \(A\) and the perpendicular from the other end \(B\) of the arc subtending the angle. In the diagram, we have \[\versin\theta = \frac{AD}{R}; \text{ and } AD = R\versin\theta.\]

The line \(AD\) is always drawn in one direction and \(\versin\theta\) is always \(+\).

As \(\theta\) increases from \(0\) to \(\pi\), \(\versin\theta\) increases from \(0\) to \(2\); and as \(\theta\) increases from \(\pi\) to \(2\pi\), \(\versin\theta\) diminishes from \(2\) to \(0\).

The seven ratios defined above are altogether independent of the size of the circle described, and depend only on the angle. They are therefore functions of the circular measure \(\theta\), remaining the same for the same value of \(\theta\) whatever radius be taken, but changing with the value of \(\theta\); and they are numbers calculable from the number \(\theta\). The lines, to which their ratios correspond, depend partly on the value of \(\theta\) and partly on the radius, and are expressed by the radius multiplied by the corresponding circular function.

Thus if the angle \(AOB = \theta\) in the diagrams of this Chapter, \[\begin{gather*} \begin{aligned} BD &= OB \sin\theta = OD \tan\theta, \\ EB &= OB \cos\theta = EO \cot\theta, \\ AF &= OA \tan\theta = OF \sin\theta, \\ CG &= OC \cot\theta = OG \cos\theta, \end{aligned} \\ OS = OB \sec\theta,\quad OK = OB \cosec\theta. \end{gather*}\]

Relations between the circular functions of the same angle. If the angle \(AOB\) and the radius of the circle be the same in these diagrams, the triangles \(BOD\), \(FAO\), \(SOB\) are right-angled and similar. Hence expressing their sides in terms of the radius and the circular function corresponding to each, we have (Euc. I. 47) \[\begin{gather*} R^2 = R^2 \sin^2\theta + R^2 \cos^2\theta, \\ \text{or } \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1 \tag*{\normalsize(\osf{1})} \\ R^2 \sec^2\theta = R^2 + R^2 \tan^2\theta, \\ \text{or } \sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta \tag*{\normalsize(\osf{2})} \end{gather*}\] And putting \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\) for \(\theta\) in this \[\cosec^2\theta = 1 + \cot^2\theta \tag*{\normalsize(\osf{3})}\] Also (Euc. VI. 4) \(R \tan\theta: R :: R \sin\theta: R \cos\theta\), \[\begin{gather*} \text{or } \tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \tag*{\normalsize(\osf{4})} \\ R \sec\theta : R :: R : R \cos\theta, \\ \text{or } \sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta} \tag*{\normalsize(\osf{5})} \end{gather*}\] From which putting \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\) for \(\theta\), \[\begin{align*} \cotan\theta = \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} &= \frac{1}{\tan\theta} \tag*{\normalsize(\osf{6})} \\ \cosec\theta &= \frac{1}{\sin\theta} \tag*{\normalsize(\osf{7})} \end{align*}\] And \(R\versin\theta = R - R \cos\theta\) \[\text{whence } \versin\theta = 1 - \cos\theta \tag*{\normalsize(\osf{8})}\]

\Chapter{VI.}{OF LOGARITHMIC TABLES.}

\First{Tables} have been formed of the values of the circular
functions of angles at intervals of~$1'$, or in more minute
tables at intervals of~$10''$, from $0°$~to~$45°$. It is unnecessary
to calculate those of greater angles, as the angles between
$45°$ and $90°$ are complements of the angles between $0°$~and~$45°$.
Methods of calculation are given in Higher Trigonometry.
Such tables are called Tables of Natural Sines,
Cosines,~\&c. For practical calculations they are superseded
by logarithmic tables, the use of which may be shortly
explained.

Logarithms of ordinary numbers may be defined to be
numbers, so calculated from the ordinary numbers, that the
sum of the logarithms of two numbers is the logarithm of
their product. Thus, if $m$~and~$n$ be two numbers,
\begin{gather*}
\log m + \log n = \log (m × n).
\Tag{1} \\
\intertext{\indent Now}
\log (m ÷ n) + \log n = \log n (m ÷ n) = \log m; \\
\therefore \log m - \log n = \log(m ÷ n).
\Tag{2}
\end{gather*}

From~\Eq{2} it follows, putting $m = n$, that
\[
\log 1 = 0,
\Tag{3}
\]
and that the logarithm of a proper fraction is~$-$.

Also from~\Eq{1}
\begin{align*}
\log n^2 &= 2 \log n, \\
\log n^3 &= 3 \log n,\quad \text{\&c.}
\end{align*}
and, generally, $\log n^p = p \log n$, if $p$ is an integer, \\
and therefore $q \log n^{\tfrac{p}{q}} = p \log n$,
\[
\text{or } \log n^{\tfrac{p}{q}} = \frac{p}{q} × \log n.
\]

So that whether $x$ is an integer, or a fraction,
\[
\log n^x = x \log n.
\Tag{4}
\]

If $a =$ the number of which the logarithm is~$1$, $a$~is said
to be the base of the system of logarithms: then denoting
logarithms in the system of which the base is~$a$ by~$\log_a$, \Eq{4}~becomes
\[
\log_a n = x, \text{ when } a^x = n.
\Tag{5}
\]

Common logarithms are those for which the base is~$10$.

Hence in \Eq{3}~and~\Eq{5} denoting common logarithms by~$\log$;
$\log 1 = 0$; $\log 10 = 1$; $\log 100 = 2$; $\log 1000 = 3$; and so on.

Equation~\Eq{5} shews that the logarithm increases with the
number: therefore it appears that the common logarithm of
a number of one integral digit is a proper fraction; that of
a number of $2$~digits is $1 + \text{a fraction}$; of $3$~digits $2 + \text{a
fraction}$, and so on. The integral part, or \emph{characteristic}, of
the logarithm, therefore, is one less than the number of
integral digits and is known by inspection, so that it is
usual in the tables to give only the decimal part of the
logarithm, or the \emph{mantissa}.

Since also by \Eq{1}~and~\Eq{2},
\begin{align*}
\log (10^m × n) &= m + \log n,\\
\text{and }\log (n \div 10^m) &= -m + \log n,
\end{align*}
it appears that multiplication or division by any power of~$10$
will affect only the characteristic of the logarithm, and
that the decimal part of the logarithm, or mantissa, will be
the same for numbers consisting of the same succession of
digits followed or preceded by any number of ciphers, and
with a decimal point occurring between any two digits.

It will be seen that all the arithmetical operations for
calculation are simplified by the use of logarithmic tables.

Thus, with tables, the result of multiplication is calculated
by adding logarithms, of division by subtracting logarithms,
of raising to a power by multiplying a logarithm
by a number, of extracting a root by dividing a logarithm
by a number.

Calculations are thus so much abbreviated\footnote
  {Laplace has remarked with reference to the value of the invention,
  that ``by reducing to a few hours what otherwise is the labour of several
  months, it doubles, so to speak, the life of the astronomer, and spares
  him the errors and annoyance inseparable from long calculations.''}
that it is
very desirable in establishing formulæ for the calculation of
some of the sides and angles of triangles from given values
of others, that the formulæ should be adapted to logarithmic
calculation, as is done in the next chapter.

It is also necessary to have logarithmic tables of the
Trigonometrical ratios.

Since the sine of an angle is always less than 1, the
common logarithm of the sine is a $-$~number. The same is
true of the cosine, of the tangent of an angle~$< 45°$,~\&c. To
avoid the use of negative numbers, the tabular logarithms
of the circular functions are the common logarithms of
these ratios increased by~$10$: which must be remembered
in using the tables in calculations.

Where, as is generally the case in practice, the logarithm
of a given number, or, conversely, the number for a given
logarithm is not actually to be found in the tables, these
can be found approximately from the principle that, for
considerable numbers of small difference, the difference of
two numbers is nearly proportional to the difference of
their logarithms. Whence the difference between a number
and the nearest number in the tables being known, the
difference to be added to the nearest logarithm in the tables
can be approximately found, and the converse.

The same method applies also to the tabular logarithms
of the circular functions, it being generally approximately
true that the difference of two tabular logarithms of a
circular function is proportional to the difference of the
corresponding angles, when that difference is small, and the
angles are neither very small nor very near~$90°$\footnotemark.
\footnotetext{Logarithms were invented by John Napier, who was born in \Date{1550}
  and died \osf{4}th~April, \Date{1617}. He was descended from and claimed to
  represent the elder branch of the Earls of Lennox. From him are
  descended the Baronet of Milliken and the Lord Napier. But the
  inventor of Logarithms was not a Peer, and should not be styled Baron
  Napier as is often done. The mistake arises from his having been
  ``Baron'' in the sense of proprietor of the Barony of Merchistoun, near
  Edinburgh. In a paper dated \osf{23}rd~April, \Date{1584}, at Gartness on the
  Endrick (where were his Lennox Estates and where it is a local tradition
  that he calculated his Canon of Logarithms), he signs himself ``Jhone
  Neper \textit{Fear} of Merchiston.'' The word fear is the Celtic equivalent of
  Baron.

  His ``Canon,'' or table of Logarithms, was published in~\Date{1614}.}

\Chapter{VII.}{SOLUTION OF TRIANGLES.}

\First{A triangle} is said to be solved when the sides and
angles are calculated from the data.

\Paragraph{Right-Angled Triangles.} Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Let
$C = 90°$; and let $BC = a$, $CA = b$,
$AB = c$.

\begin{wrapfigure}[8]{r}{1.75in}
  \hspace*{-0.375in}\Input[2.125in]{041a}
\end{wrapfigure}

Then if the side $AB$ be taken
as radius, the ratio of $BC$ to $AB$
is the sine of~$A$; and of $AC$ to
$AB$ is its cosine; or
\begin{align*}
a &= c \sin A;\quad b = c \cos A. \\
\intertext{Similarly}
b &= c \sin B;\quad a = c \cos B.
\end{align*}

If $AC$ be taken as radius, since $CB$ touches the arc
described, the ratio of $CB$ to $CA$ is the tangent, and of $AB$
to $CA$ is secant of~$A$; so that
\begin{align*}
a &= b \tan A; \quad c = b \sec A. \\
\intertext{\indentAnd similarly }
b &= a \tan B; \quad c = a \sec B.
\end{align*}

From these equations, it is easy logarithmically to solve
a right-angled triangle when a side and an angle, or when
two sides are given.

\Paragraph{Given $c$ and $A$}, we have $B = 90° - A$,
\begin{align*}
\log a &= \log c + \tab\log \sin A - 10, \\
\log b &= \log c + \tab\log \cos A - 10;
\end{align*}
whence $B$, $a$, $b$ are found.

\Paragraph{Given $a$ and $A$}, we have $B = 90°- A$,
\begin{align*}
\log b &= \log a + \tab\log \tan B - 10, \\
\log c &= \log a + \tab\log \sec B - 10;
\end{align*}
whence $B$, $c$, $b$ are found.

\Paragraph{Given $c$ and $a$}, we have
\begin{align*}
&\begin{aligned}
  \tab\log \sin A &= 10 + \log a - \log c, \\
                B &= 90° - A,
\end{aligned} \\
&\log b = \log c + \tab \log \cos A - 10;
\end{align*}
whence $A$, $B$, $b$ are found.

\Paragraph{Triangles not Right-Angled.}

Case~I\@. Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle, $ABC'$
\begin{figure}[hbt]
  \begin{center}
    \Input[\linewidth]{042a}
  \end{center}
\end{figure}
a triangle having an obtuse angle at~$C'$. In both triangles
draw $AD$ perpendicular to $BC$ produced if necessary.
Then in both triangles, if $AB$ be taken as radius,
\[
AD = AB \sin B = c \sin B;
\]
and if $CA$ be taken as radius,
\[
AD = CA \sin C = b \sin C.
\]

Hence
\begin{gather*}
  b \sin C = c \sin B, \\
  \text{or } \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}.
\end{gather*}

If the perpendicular had been drawn from $B$ to $CA$ we
should similarly have got
\begin{gather*}
  \frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{c}{\sin C}\;, \\
\text{so that }
\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}\;,
\end{gather*}
or \emph{the sides are proportional to the sines of the opposite angles}.
This is true of all triangles. Hence we can logarithmically
solve a triangle when a side and the opposite angle are
given, and likewise another side or another angle.

\Paragraph{Given $C$ and $c$, and $b$.}
\[
\Tab\log\sin B = (\tab\log\sin C - \log c) + \log b,
\]
a logarithmic equation for the determination of~$B$.

There is but one acute angle which can have its sine
of a particular value: so that, if we know $B$ to be acute,
there is but one value of~$B$ to be taken. And if $b < c$ the
angle~$B$ must be acute; and we find it by means of the
equation.

Then
\[
A = 180° - (B + C),
\]
and
\[
\log a = \tab\log\sin A - (\tab\log\sin C - \log c),
\]
so that the triangle is solved.

If however $b > c$, we do not know that $B$~is acute, and
as the sine of the supplement of an acute angle is the same
as the sine of the angle, there are two values of~$B$, the one
less than~$90°$, the other its supplement, which satisfy the
above logarithmic relation. That is, there is an \emph{ambiguity}
as to the value of~$B$. There will always be this ambiguity
in determining the angle of a triangle from its sine, unless
there be something to point out whether the angle is acute
or obtuse: and therefore it is generally inconvenient to use
a method involving the determination of the angle from its
sine. But in this instance there is a real \emph{geometrical} ambiguity.
For if we construct a triangle with its angle
$ACB = C$, its side $CA = b$, and the side opposite $C = c$, it is
evident that, if $c$ be $< b$, there are two triangles $AB_1C$ and
$AB_2C$ corresponding to the data. The angle opposite $CA$
in the one of these is acute $= B_1$; in the other it is obtuse
$= B_2$. But since $AB_1 = AB_2$, $B_2 = 180° - B_1$. In this case
\begin{figure}[hbt]
  \begin{center}
    \Input{044a}
  \end{center}
\end{figure}
therefore, \emph{where two sides and the angle opposite the less are
given}, which is called the \emph{ambiguous case}, there are two
triangles. The acute angle~$B_1$ can be found from the
formula
\[
\tab\log\sin B_1 = \log b + (\tab\log\sin C - \log c),
\]
and then $B_2 = 180° - B$.

If $A_1$ and $A_2$ are the corresponding values of the third
angle $a_1$,~$a_2$ of the third side,
\[
A_1 = 180° - (B_1 + C);\quad A_2 = 180° - (B_2 + C),
\]
and
\begin{gather*}
\log a_1 = \tab\log\sin A_1 - (\tab\log\sin C - \log c), \\
\log a_2 = \tab\log\sin A_2 - (\tab\log\sin C - \log c).
\end{gather*}

Case~II\@. Let $ABC$ be a triangle: and let $CB$ be
greater than~$CA$.

\begin{figure}[hbt]
  \begin{center}
    \Input{045a}
  \end{center}
\end{figure}
From $C$ as centre with $CB$~as radius, describe the circle
$DBE$. Produce $BA$ to meet its circumference in~$F$, and
$CA$ both ways to meet it in $E$~and~$D$.

Join $FC$, $BD$, $BE$, $BF$.

Then $DBE$ is a right angle; and
\[
DCB = A + B = 2BED;
\]
also
\[
A = ECF + CFA = ECF + B,
\]
and
\[
ECF = A - B = 2FBE.
\]

So that $BED = \dfrac{1}{2}(A + B)$; $FBE = \dfrac{1}{2}(A - B)$.

And $BDA$ is the complement of $BED$, $ABD$ of $FBE$.

Now in the triangle $DBA$,
\[
\frac{DA}{\sin ABD} = \frac{BA}{\sin BDA},\quad\text{or}\quad
\frac{a+b}{\cos\dfrac{1}{2}(A - B)} = \frac{c}{\cos\dfrac{1}{2}(A + B)}.
\]

\[
\frac{EA}{\sin FBE} = \frac{AB}{\sin BED},\quad\text{or}\quad
\frac{a-b}{\sin\dfrac{1}{2}(A - B)} = \frac{c}{\sin\dfrac{1}{2}(A + B)}.
\]

By combining these and remembering that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$
we get
\[
\frac{\tan\dfrac{1}{2}(A - B)}{\tan\dfrac{1}{2}(A + B)}
  = \frac{a - b}{a + b}.
\]

These relations give the simplest logarithmic solution
of a triangle, when two sides and the contained angle are
given\footnotemark.
\footnotetext{These formulæ are given in p.~\osf{13} of Thacker's \textit{Miscellany}, \Date{1743}.
  Their application to the solution of triangles was pointed out by
  Professor Wallace, of Edinburgh, in the \textit{Transactions, R.S.E.}, \Date{1823}.}

\Paragraph{Given $a$,~$b$, and~$C$}, we have
\[
A + B = 180° - C, \text{ so that } \frac{1}{2} (A + B) \text{ is known}.
\]

Then
\begin{multline*}
\tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} (A - B) = \tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} (A + B) \\
+ \log (a - b) - \log (a + b),
\end{multline*}
which determines the acute angle $\dfrac{1}{2} (A - B)$.

Whence
\begin{align*}
  A &= \frac{1}{2} (A + B) + \frac{1}{2} (A - B) \\
\intertext{and}
  B &= \frac{1}{2} (A + B) - \frac{1}{2} (A - B)
\end{align*}
are found.

The third side $c$ could now be found from the relation
$\log c = \tab\log\sin C - (\tab\log\sin A - \log a)$, but it is shorter
in practice to determine~$c$ either from
\[
\log c
  = \tab\log\cos \frac{1}{2} (A + B)
  - \tab\log\cos \frac{1}{2} (A - B) + \log (a + b),
\]
or from
\[
\log c
  = \tab\log\sin \frac{1}{2} (A + B)
  - \tab\log\sin \frac{1}{2} (A - B) + \log (a - b),
\]

Thus when two unequal sides and the angle between
them are given, the other side and other angles are found.

If an angle and two equal sides containing it are given,
the remaining angles are each the complement of half
the given angle, and the third side can be found as in
Case~I\@.

Case~III\@. Let $ABC$ be the triangle, $O$~the centre of
the inscribed circle, so that $AO, BO, CO$ bisect the angles,
\begin{figure}[hbt]
  \begin{center}
    \Input{047a}
  \end{center}
\end{figure}
and the perpendiculars $Oa, Ob, Oc$ are each of them a radius
of the inscribed circle.

Let this radius $= r$, let the sum of the sides $a + b + c = 2s$;
then (Chapter~\Rom{II}.)
\[
Ab = Ac = s - a,\quad
Bc = Ba = s - b,\quad
Ca = Cb = s - c.
\]

And in the right-angled triangles $AOb$, $BOc$, $COa$,
we have
\begin{gather*}
r = (s - a) \tan \frac{1}{2} A
  = (s - b) \tan \frac{1}{2} B
  = (s - c) \tan \frac{1}{2} C, \\
\text{where } r^2 = \frac{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}{s}.
\end{gather*}

From these the angles may be found when the sides are
given.

\Paragraph{Given $a, b, c$}, we get the logarithmic relations
\[
\log r = \frac{1}{2} \bigl\{
  \log (s - a) + \log (s - b) + \log (s - c) - \log s
\bigr\},
\]
and
\begin{align*}
\tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} A &= 10 + \log r - \log (s - a), \\
\tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} B &= 10 + \log r - \log (s - b), \\
\tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} C &= 10 + \log r - \log (s - c),
\end{align*}
whence the three angles are easily found. There is also a
simple verification of the process afforded by taking the sum
of the three angles, which ought to be~$180°$\footnotemark.
\footnotetext{The formulæ used here were discovered by William Purser of Dublin,
  in \Date{1632}. Consult Wallace's \textit{Geometrical Theorems}.}

Now in the triangle \(DBA\), \[\frac{DA}{\sin ABD} = \frac{BA}{\sin BDA},\quad\text{or}\quad \frac{a+b}{\cos\dfrac{1}{2}(A - B)} = \frac{c}{\cos\dfrac{1}{2}(A + B)}.\]

And in the triangle \(BAE\), \[\frac{EA}{\sin FBE} = \frac{AB}{\sin BED},\quad\text{or}\quad \frac{a-b}{\sin\dfrac{1}{2}(A - B)} = \frac{c}{\sin\dfrac{1}{2}(A + B)}.\]

By combining these and remembering that \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) we get \[\frac{\tan\dfrac{1}{2}(A - B)}{\tan\dfrac{1}{2}(A + B)} = \frac{a - b}{a + b}.\]

These relations give the simplest logarithmic solution of a triangle, when two sides and the contained angle are given. 10

Given \(a\), \(b\), and \(C\), we have \[A + B = 180° - C, \text{ so that } \frac{1}{2} (A + B) \text{ is known}.\]

Then \[\begin{gather*} \tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} (A - B) = \tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} (A + B) \\ + \log (a - b) - \log (a + b), \end{gather*}\] which determines the acute angle \(\dfrac{1}{2} (A - B)\).

Whence \[\begin{align*} A &= \frac{1}{2} (A + B) + \frac{1}{2} (A - B) \\ \\ \text{and} B &= \frac{1}{2} (A + B) - \frac{1}{2} (A - B) \end{align*}\] are found.

The third side \(c\) could now be found from the relation \(\log c = \tab\log\sin C - (\tab\log\sin A - \log a)\), but it is shorter in practice to determine \(c\) either from \[\log c = \tab\log\cos \frac{1}{2} (A + B) - \tab\log\cos \frac{1}{2} (A - B) + \log (a + b),\] or from \[\log c = \tab\log\sin \frac{1}{2} (A + B) - \tab\log\sin \frac{1}{2} (A - B) + \log (a - b),\]

Thus when two unequal sides and the angle between them are given, the other side and other angles are found.

If an angle and two equal sides containing it are given, the remaining angles are each the complement of half the given angle, and the third side can be found as in Case I.

Case III. Let \(ABC\) be the triangle, \(O\) the centre of the inscribed circle, so that \(AO, BO, CO\) bisect the angles,

and the perpendiculars \(Oa, Ob, Oc\) are each of them a radius of the inscribed circle.

Let this radius \(= r\), let the sum of the sides \(a + b + c = 2s\); then (Chapter ii.) \[Ab = Ac = s - a,\quad Bc = Ba = s - b,\quad Ca = Cb = s - c.\]

And in the right-angled triangles \(AOb\), \(BOc\), \(COa\), we have \[\begin{gather*} r = (s - a) \tan \frac{1}{2} A = (s - b) \tan \frac{1}{2} B = (s - c) \tan \frac{1}{2} C, \\ \text{where } r^2 = \frac{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}{s}. \end{gather*}\]

From these the angles may be found when the sides are given.

Given \(a, b, c\), we get the logarithmic relations \[\log r = \frac{1}{2} \bigl\{ \log (s - a) + \log (s - b) + \log (s - c) - \log s \bigr\},\] and \[\begin{align*} \tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} A &= 10 + \log r - \log (s - a), \\ \tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} B &= 10 + \log r - \log (s - b), \\ \tab\log\tan \frac{1}{2} C &= 10 + \log r - \log (s - c), \end{align*}\] whence the three angles are easily found. There is also a simple verification of the process afforded by taking the sum of the three angles, which ought to be \(180°\). 11

\Chapter{VIII.}{OF TRIGONOMETRICAL SURVEYING.}

\First{In}  last Chapter methods have been given of calculating
the remaining parts of a triangle when one side and two
other parts of the triangle are previously known.

In Geodesy, or the application of this part of Trigonometry
to surveying, a line, called \emph{the Base}, is measured
between two convenient stations; and the angles between
lines from these stations to points visible from the stations
are measured with appropriate instruments. With these
data calculations are made of the distances between new
stations, where additional angles may be observed and the
operations repeated as often as required. The angles measured
by instruments are of three classes.

\No{1} Horizontal angles, or angles in the horizontal plane
through the station.

The horizontal angle between two objects is the angle
between the vertical planes through the station and each
object: it is also called the angle in azimuth.

\No{2} Vertical angles, or angles in a vertical plane through
the station.

The angle of elevation (or depression) of an object, also
called its altitude, is the vertical angle between the horizontal
line and the line from the station to the object.

\No{3} Angles in planes neither horizontal nor vertical.

The angle between two objects is the angle between
the lines from the station to each object. This angle is in
the plane through the station and the two objects.

In land surveying the angles measured belong to the
first or second class, and are measured with a Theodolite
or similar instrument.

Angles of the third class are usually measured with a
Sextant or similar instrument.

For details of the measurement of a base, and a description
of the instruments principally employed in practical
surveying, the reader is referred to Professor Rankine's
\textit{Manual of Civil Engineering}, Part~\osf{1}. \textit{Of Engineering Geodesy},
and for the methods employed in a great Trigonometrical
survey to the Ordnance Survey \textit{Account of the
Principal Triangulation}, published by the Board of Ordnance,
\Date{1858}. Assuming, however, that a base line and angles can
be accurately measured by appropriate instruments, it seems
within the scope of this elementary treatise to give instances
of the determination of heights and distances from such
measurements.

I\@. The distance between two stations $A$~and~$B$, visible
from each other, being ascertained, and the angles between
a visible object~$C$ and the other station being measured at
each station, the distances $AC$~and~$BC$ can be found by
Case~I\@.

In this instance the angles measured are in the plane
through $A$,~$B$,~$C$.

If the angle of elevation of $C$ be likewise measured at
either station, the height of~$C$ above that station can be
found by solving a right-angled triangle of which the hypotenuse
and one of the acute angles are known.

When the horizontal distance of the stations is given
and is in a vertical plane through~$C$, only vertical angles
are required and the work is simplified; and when in addition
one station is in the vertical line through~$C$ (which
is then said to be ``accessible'') the measurement of one
vertical angle and the solution of one right-angled triangle
determine the height of~$C$.

II\@. From each of two stations $A$~and~$B$, visible from
each other, and at a known distance, the angles between
the other station and two objects $C$~and~$D$ are measured.
Then the triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$ can be solved (by
Case~I.), and the distances $AC$, $BC$, $AD$, $BD$ are found.

If in addition the angles between $C$~and~$D$ are measured
at either station, the distance $CD$ can be found by Case~II\@.

If the survey extends over so small a fraction of the
earth's surface that the vertical lines over the whole may
be considered perpendicular to one horizontal plane, and if
the distances measured or calculated are the \emph{horizontal distances}
of the points (or the ``projections'' of the actual distances
on the horizontal plane), which is the case when
the survey is conducted for the purpose of making a plan;
then the angles to be measured will all be horizontal angles,
and the work will be simpler. And if in addition the angle
of elevation of any point be observed from a known horizontal
distance, the height of the point above the horizontal
plane of reference (which may be ``the level of the sea'')
can be found by the solution of a right-angled triangle.

Where the extent of the earth's surface surveyed is too
great for the above supposition, the calculations have to be
corrected for the sphericity of the earth (see books on
Spherical Trigonometry), and in very great and very accurate
surveys also for the earth's deviation from a perfect
sphere. (See the \textit{Principal Triangulation} of the Ordnance
Survey.)

\Chapter{IX.}{OF PROJECTIONS.}

\First{The} point where the perpendicular from a given point
on a given plane or a given line meets the plane or line
is called the projection (or more precisely the orthogonal
projection) of the point on the plane or line.

The part of one line intercepted between the projections
on it of the extremities of another line, or of a broken line,
is called the projection of the second line, or broken line,
on the first.

It is convenient to take one direction of the line of projection
(say from left to right) as the $+$ direction and the
opposite as the $-$~direction; also to consider one end of
the projected line as its beginning; and to measure the
inclination of the two lines by the angle between the projected
line and a line drawn from its beginning parallel to
the line of projection and in the $+$~direction.

\Prop{I}{The projection of a line on a given line is equal
to the projected line multiplied by the cosine of the angle between
the lines.}

\begin{figure}[hbt]
  \begin{center}
    \Input[\linewidth]{052a}
  \end{center}
\end{figure}
Let $AB$ be the projected line, $X'X$~the line of projection;
then in each case, $A'B'$~being the projection, we have
\[
A'B'= AB \cos BAC.
\]

If $BAC$ be acute, $\cos BAC$ is~$+$, and $A'B'$ is~$+$ and is
measured from~$A'$ in the $+$~direction; but if $BAC$ be obtuse,
$\cos BAC$ is~$-$, and $A'B'$ is~$-$ and is measured from~$A'$
in the $-$~direction.

\Prop{II}{The projection of a broken line is the algebraic
sum of the projections of the parts of which it is made up.}

\begin{figure}[hbt]
  \begin{center}
    \Input{052b}
  \end{center}
\end{figure}

Let $ABCD$ be a broken line, made up of the parts $AB$,
$BC$, $CD$. Let $A'B'$, $B'C'$, $C'D'$ be the projections of these
parts on $X'X$. Thus $A'D'$ is the projection of the broken
line. And
\[
A'D' = A'B' + B'C' + C'D'
\]
both in the case where all these projections are~$+$ and also
where, as in the figure, $B'C'$~is~$-$.

chapters.text_html:
CHAPTER X.

THE SINE AND COSINE OF THE SUM AND DIFFERENCE OF TWO ANGLES.

. To find the sine and cosine of the sum of two angles.

r2.25in

Let \(C\) be the centre of a circle of which the radius \(CA = R\).

Let the circular measure of \(ACB = \theta\), and of \(BCD = \phi\).

Then \(\theta + \phi\) is the circular measure of \(ACD\).

Draw \(DE\), \(DF\) perpendicular to \(CA\), \(CB\).

Then \[\begin{align*} &&DE &= R \sin (\theta + \phi); & CE &= R \cos (\theta + \phi); &&\\ &&DF &= R \sin \phi; & CF &= R \cos \phi. && \end{align*}\]

But \(DE\) is the projection of the broken line \(CFD\) on \(DE\); therefore \[\begin{gather*} \begin{aligned} DE &= \text{projection of } CF + \text{projection of } FD \\ &= CF \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) + FD \cos\theta \\ &= CF \sin\theta + FD \cos\theta, \\ \end{aligned} \\ \begin{aligned} \text{i.e.\ } R \sin (\theta + \phi) &= R \cos\phi \sin\theta + R \sin\phi \cos\theta, \\ \text{or\ } \sin (\theta + \phi) &= \sin\theta \cos\phi + \cos\theta \sin\phi. \end{aligned} \end{gather*}\]

Again, \(CE\) is the projection of the broken line \(CFD\) on \(CA\), \[\begin{gather*} \begin{aligned} \therefore CE &= \text{projection of } CF + \text{projection of } FD \\ &= CF \cos\theta + FD \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \theta\right) \\ &= CF \cos\theta - FD \sin\theta; \end{aligned} \\ \begin{aligned} \text{i.e.\ } R \cos (\theta + \phi) &= R \cos\phi \cos\theta - R \sin\phi \sin\theta, \\ \text{or } \cos (\theta + \phi) &= \cos\theta \cos\phi - \sin\theta \sin\phi. \end{aligned} \end{gather*}\]

. To find the sine and cosine of the difference of two angles.

r2.25in

Let \[\begin{align*} \theta &= \text{circular measure of ACB}, \\ \phi &= \text{% % \text{\cdots}% of BCD.} \end{align*}\]

Then \(\theta - \phi =\) circular measure of \(ACD\).

Draw \(DE\), \(DF\) perpendicular to \(CA\), \(CB\).

Then

\[\begin{align*} &&DE &= R \sin (\theta - \phi); &&&&\\ &&CE &= R \cos (\theta - \phi); &&&&\\ &&CF &= R \cos \phi; & FD &= R \sin \phi.&& \end{align*}\]

But \(DE\) is the projection of \(CFD\) on \(DE\) \[\begin{gather*} \begin{aligned} &= \text{projection of } CF + \text{projection of } FD \\ &= CF \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) + FD \cos (\pi - \theta) \\ &= CF \sin \theta - FD \cos \theta; \end{aligned} \\ \begin{aligned} \text{i.e.\ } R \sin (\theta - \phi) &= R \cos\phi \sin\theta - R \sin\phi \cos\theta, \\ \text{or } \sin (\theta - \phi) &= \sin\theta \cos\phi - \cos\theta \sin\phi. \end{aligned} \end{gather*}\]

Again, \(CE\) is the projection of \(CFD\) on \(CA\) \[\begin{gather*} \begin{aligned} &= \text{projection of } CF + \text{projection of } FD \\ &= CF \cos \theta + FD \cos \left(\theta - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ &= CF \cos \theta + FD \sin \theta; \end{aligned} \\ \begin{aligned} \text{i.e.\ } R \cos (\theta - \phi) &= R \cos\phi \cos\theta + R \sin\phi \sin\theta, \\ \text{or } \cos (\theta - \phi) &= \cos\phi \cos\theta + \sin\phi \sin\theta. \end{aligned} \end{gather*}\]

The four expressions for \(\sin (\theta ± \phi)\) and \(\cos (\theta ± \phi)\) are true for all values of \(\theta\) and \(\phi\), though the diagrams suppose the angles all acute. They form the fundamental formulæ of Analytical Trigonometry.

APPENDIX. (Note to p. 10.)

To shew that, when the difference between \(R\) and \(r\) is small, the limit of each radius is very nearly \(= \dfrac{1}{3}(r + 2R)\).

Let \(r_1, r_2, \dots\) be the radii of the circles inscribed in the successive polygons, and \(R_1, R_2, \dots\) of those circumscribed about the same. Let also the limit of both be called \(r_\infty\).

Let \(R - r = 2\delta\); then \(r_1 = \dfrac{R + r}{2} = r + \delta = R - \delta\).

Let \[\begin{align*} r_2 &= r_1 + \delta_1;\quad r_3 = r_2 + \delta_2;\quad \text{\&c.} \\ \\ \text{ Then} r_\infty &= r + \delta + \delta_1 + \delta_2 + \text{\&c.\ \textit{ad inf.}} \\ \\ \text{ Also} R &= r + 2\delta;\quad R_1 = r_1 + 2\delta_1;\quad \text{\&c.} \\ \\ \text{and} R &= r_1 + \delta;\quad R_1 = r_2 + \delta_1;\quad \text{\&c.} \\ \\ \text{ But} R_1^2 &= r_1R;\quad \text{or } (r_1 + 2\delta_1)^2 = r_1(r_1 + \delta); \\ \end{align*}\] \[\begin{gather*} \therefore 4r_1\delta_1 + 4\delta_1^2 = r_1\delta; \\ \therefore \delta_1 = \frac{\delta}{4} - \frac{\delta_1^2}{r_1} < \frac{\delta}{4} > \frac{\delta}{4} - \frac{\delta_1^2}{r}; \\ \therefore \delta_1 < \frac{\delta}{4} > \frac{\delta}{4} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\delta}{4}\right)^2. \\ \\ \text{ Similarly} \delta_2 < \frac{\delta_1}{4} > \frac{\delta_1}{4} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\delta_1}{4}\right)^2 > \frac{\delta_1}{4} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\delta}{4^2}\right)^2, \\ \delta_3 < \frac{\delta_2}{4} > \frac{\delta_2}{4} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\delta_2}{4}\right)^2 > \frac{\delta_2}{4} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\delta}{4^3}\right)^2, \\ \delta_4 < \frac{\delta_3}{4} > \frac{\delta_3}{4} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\delta_3}{4}\right)^2 > \frac{\delta_3}{4} - \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\delta}{4^4}\right)^2, \\ \text{\&c.\qquad\qquad\qquad \&c.} \\ \therefore \delta + \delta_1 + \delta_2 + \dots \text{ \textit{ad inf.}} < \delta + \frac{\delta}{4} + \frac{\delta_1}{4} + \frac{\delta_2}{4} + \dots \text{ \textit{ad inf.}} \end{gather*}\] and \[\therefore \frac{3}{4}\{\delta + \delta_1 + \delta_2 + \dots \text{ \textit{ad inf.}}\} < \delta,\] or \[\delta + \delta_1 + \delta_2 + \dots < \frac{4}{3}\, \delta.\]

And \[\begin{gather*} \delta + \delta_1 + \delta_2 + \dots > \delta + \frac{\delta}{4} + \frac{\delta_1}{4} + \text{ \&c.\ \textit{ad inf.}} \\ - \frac{1}{r} \left\{ \left(\frac{\delta}{4}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\delta}{4^2}\right)^2 + \dots \text{ \textit{ad inf.}}\right\}; \end{gather*}\] \[\begin{gather*} \therefore \frac{3}{4}(\delta + \delta_1 + \delta_2 + \dots) > \delta - \frac{\delta^2}{16r} × \frac{16}{15} > \delta - \frac{\delta^2}{15r}; \\ \therefore \delta + \delta_1 + \delta_2 + \dots \text{ \textit{ad inf.}} > \frac{4}{3}\, \delta - \frac{4}{45}· \frac{\delta^2}{r}; \end{gather*}\]

\[\begin{align*} \therefore r_\infty &< r + \frac{4}{3} \delta & &> r + \frac{4}{3}\, \delta - \frac{4}{45}\, \frac{\delta^2}{r}, \\ &< \frac{1}{3} (r + 2R) & &> \frac{1}{3} (r + 2R) - \frac{(R - r)^2}{45r}. \end{align*}\]

So that when, as in the text, \(R - r < .00003\) the error in taking the ultimate radius \(= \dfrac{1}{3}(r + 2R)\) is \(< \dfrac{.0000000009}{45r}\) which does not affect the tenth decimal place.
